title: The Twelve-Factor App, by Adam Wiggins (12factor.net)
text: The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology by Adam Wiggins, drawn from Heroku's experience deploying hundreds of thousands of software-as-a-service applications, for building portable and scalable cloud applications independent of language and backing services. Its stated goals are minimizing onboarding friction, offering maximum portability across execution environments, being suitable for deployment on modern cloud platforms, minimizing divergence between development and production for continuous deployment, and scaling up without significant changes to architecture. The twelve factors are: I Codebase, one codebase tracked in version control with many deploys; II Dependencies, explicitly declare and isolate dependencies rather than relying on system-wide packages; III Config, store environment-specific configuration in environment variables, never hardcoded, so the same build runs in every environment; IV Backing Services, treat databases, caches, and queues as attached, swappable resources rather than integral parts of the app; V Build, release, run, strictly separate the build stage that compiles code, the release stage that combines the build with config, and the run stage that executes processes; VI Processes, run the app as one or more stateless processes, keeping any state in a backing service; VII Port binding, be self-contained and export services via port binding rather than relying on an injected application server; VIII Concurrency, scale out horizontally through the process model; IX Disposability, maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown; X Dev/prod parity, keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible; XI Logs, treat logs as event streams written to stdout and let the execution environment aggregate them; XII Admin processes, run administrative and management tasks as one-off processes using the same codebase and config as regular processes.

title: OWASP Top 10:2021 (owasp.org)
text: The OWASP Top 10 is a standard awareness document for developers and web application security, representing a broad consensus about the most critical security risks to web applications. In the 2021 edition the ranked categories are: A01 Broken Access Control, addressing improper enforcement of authorization so users can act outside their intended permissions; A02 Cryptographic Failures, covering weak or missing protection of sensitive data in transit and at rest; A03 Injection, where untrusted input is interpreted as commands or queries, a category that in 2021 also absorbed cross-site scripting; A04 Insecure Design, a category focused on missing or ineffective security controls, secure design patterns, and threat modeling during the development phase rather than implementation bugs; A05 Security Misconfiguration, covering insecure default settings and improperly configured systems; A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components, addressing risks from dependencies that are unpatched or unsupported; A07 Identification and Authentication Failures, covering weaknesses in identity verification, credential management, and session handling; A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures, addressing insecure update and deployment pipelines, unsigned or unverified updates, and untrusted deserialization; A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures, involving insufficient detection, alerting, and response visibility; and A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), where a server is tricked into making unauthorized requests to internal or external resources. Insecure Design and Software and Data Integrity Failures were new categories in 2021, and SSRF was added based on the community survey. The document is intended to help backend developers build security into applications systematically.

title: Microservices, by James Lewis and Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com)
text: Lewis and Fowler define the microservice architectural style as an approach to developing a single application as a suite of small services, each running in its own process and communicating with lightweight mechanisms, often an HTTP resource API. They identify nine common characteristics. Componentization via Services makes components independently deployable and replaceable out-of-process units rather than in-process libraries, so one service can be updated without redeploying the whole application. Organized around Business Capabilities structures cross-functional teams around business domains instead of technology layers, counteracting Conway's Law. Products not Projects means a team owns a service over its full lifetime, following the you-build-it-you-run-it idea. Smart Endpoints and Dumb Pipes puts logic in the services and uses simple protocols like HTTP and lightweight messaging rather than a complex enterprise service bus. Decentralized Governance favors emergent standards and lets teams choose the right tools and languages for each problem. Decentralized Data Management lets each service manage its own database and encourages polyglot persistence, accepting eventual consistency and compensating transactions over distributed transactions. Infrastructure Automation relies on continuous delivery, automated testing, and deployment pipelines to manage operational complexity. Design for Failure requires services to tolerate the failure of others, with real-time monitoring and resilience patterns because distributed calls can fail. Evolutionary Design treats service boundaries as refactorable, using decomposition to control change so services can be replaced or upgraded independently. The authors note microservices are not a free lunch and warn about the added complexity of distributed systems.

title: Conway's Law, by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com)
text: Conway's Law, first stated by Melvin Conway in 1968, holds that any organization that designs a system will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure. Martin Fowler explains that software architectures inevitably mirror the teams that build them: a single team tends to produce a streamlined design, while splitting work across teams reproduces that split in the system, the classic example being a two-team group that writes a two-pass compiler. The mechanism is human communication. Quoting colleague Chris Ford, software coupling is enabled and encouraged by human communication, so developers naturally couple their code to systems whose creators they can easily talk to, carrying over shared assumptions both through explicit function calls and through implicitly aligned mental models. Fowler describes three responses to the law. Ignoring it invites friction when team structure and desired architecture diverge. Accepting it means consciously aligning architecture with communication patterns. The Inverse Conway Maneuver is the most proactive: deliberately restructuring the development organization to encourage the desired software architecture, an approach common in microservices work where autonomous, capability-centric teams produce independently deployable services. For a technical lead the strategic implication is that modular decomposition and organizational structure must evolve together. Small co-located teams face few constraints, while geographically distributed teams need well-defined and limited interfaces, and a mismatch between team topology and architecture creates persistent friction that requires adjusting both the organization and the technical design at once. The page was published on October 20, 2022 and revised October 24, 2022.

title: Is High Quality Software Worth the Cost?, by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com)
text: Martin Fowler argues that the usual tradeoff between software quality and cost is largely a false one, because quality has two very different meanings. External quality is what users can see: the user interface, reliability, and absence of defects, and customers can rationally weigh whether more of it is worth a higher price. Internal quality is the architecture and organization of the code, which users never observe directly, so its value cannot be judged by looking at the running product. Fowler presents the Design Stamina Hypothesis as a pseudo-graph of cumulative functionality over time: neglecting internal quality lets a team move faster at first, but accumulating cruft steadily slows the addition of new features, while investing in internal quality costs a little up front and then keeps or even increases delivery speed. The crossover point where good design pays off comes surprisingly early, and he notes that developers find poor quality code significantly slows them down within a few weeks, so attention to internal quality pays off in weeks not months. The central insight reframes the debate entirely: because better internal quality makes adding new features easier, and therefore quicker and cheaper, spending effort on clear code, refactoring, testing, and modular design is sound economics rather than gold plating. He acknowledges that even elite teams inevitably create some cruft as they learn and as requirements change, but systematic attention to quality prevents that cruft from compounding. The article was published on May 29, 2019.

title: Software Architecture Guide, by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com)
text: In his Software Architecture Guide, Martin Fowler frames architecture as fundamentally about recognizing what is important. Drawing on correspondence with Ralph Johnson, he moves past the common notion that architecture is the set of design decisions made early in a project, which Johnson reframes as the decisions you wish you could get right early in a project, and past the idea that architecture is simply the parts that are hard to change. Two of Johnson's formulations anchor the guide: architecture is the shared understanding that the expert developers have of the system design, and architecture is about the important stuff, whatever that is. The architect's core responsibility, then, is to identify which elements matter most and to keep those elements in sound condition as the system evolves. Architecture matters because poor decisions accumulate as cruft, the internal-quality debt that obstructs developer comprehension and slows the delivery of new features. Fowler stresses that internal quality inverts the usual quality economics: while external quality often costs more to achieve, high internal quality leads to faster delivery of new features because there is less cruft to work around, and attention to internal quality pays off in weeks not months. The role of an architect is therefore less about issuing top-down mandates and more about recognizing which elements are likely to cause serious problems if left uncontrolled, and cultivating the team's shared capacity to preserve them, which makes architecture inseparable from the ongoing programming work itself.

title: Prompting best practices (Claude / Anthropic documentation, platform.claude.com)
text: Anthropic's prompting best practices lay out general techniques that apply across current Claude models. Be clear and direct: treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context, be specific about the desired output format and constraints, and explicitly request above-and-beyond behavior rather than relying on the model to infer it. The golden rule is that if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by your prompt, Claude will be too. Add context and motivation, explaining why a behavior matters, because Claude generalizes from the reasoning. Use examples effectively, since a few well-crafted examples (few-shot or multishot prompting) reliably steer output format, tone, and structure; make examples relevant, diverse, and structured, wrapping them in example tags, with three to five examples recommended. Structure prompts with XML tags so Claude can unambiguously separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs, using consistent descriptive tag names and nesting where content has a hierarchy. Give Claude a role via the system prompt to focus behavior and tone. For long context (20k or more tokens), place longform documents near the top of the prompt above the query, which can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, wrap each document in document tags with document_content and source subtags, and ask Claude to ground responses in quotes it extracts first. To control formatting, tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do and match your prompt style to the desired output. The guidance also covers leveraging adaptive thinking and chain-of-thought, chaining complex prompts where the most common pattern is self-correction (draft, review against criteria, refine), and building agentic systems with state tracking across multiple context windows. Note that prefilled assistant responses on the final turn are no longer supported starting with Claude 4.6 models.

title: Building LLM applications for production, by Chip Huyen (huyenchip.com)
text: Chip Huyen's essay on building LLM applications for production identifies natural-language ambiguity as the central obstacle to productionizing prompts. Unlike code, an accidentally changed prompt still runs but gives very different outputs, producing two failure modes: unpredictable output formats that break downstream systems, and inconsistent user experience from stochastic behavior, which setting temperature to zero only partly mitigates. On prompting versus finetuning, she notes prompting suits low-data scenarios while finetuning needs hundreds of examples to help meaningfully, citing research that a prompt is worth approximately 100 examples, and that finetuning can cut inference cost, potentially saving about $2,000 per million predictions on GPT-3.5-turbo by removing 1,000 prompt tokens per call. On economics, experimentation is cheap: running 25 prompt variants over 20 examples on GPT-4 costs roughly $300, but production dominates, and she illustrates that at $0.004 per prediction, hypothetically serving DoorDash's 10 billion daily predictions would cost $40 million a day. Output length drives latency more than input length: her tests show one-token outputs averaging 580ms versus over 1,400ms for 26-token outputs, and API providers offered no latency SLA at the time. She distinguishes prompt tuning (adjusting prompt embeddings, better than prompt engineering on models like T5 but needing embedding access) and distillation, noting Stanford's Alpaca finetuned LLaMA-7B on 52k instruction-output pairs generated by text-davinci-003 for under $500 in generation plus under $100 in finetuning. Finally she frames task composability: applications decompose into tasks orchestrated by control flows that are sequential, parallel, conditional, or iterative; agents are applications that execute multiple tasks via a specified control flow, and tools are capabilities like SQL executors, browsers, or calculators, with the model itself able to decide the control flow.

title: Prompt engineering guide (OpenAI developer documentation)
text: OpenAI's prompt engineering guide describes techniques for steering models through structured messages and context. It emphasizes message roles and instruction following: the instructions parameter provides high-level guidance on how the model should behave while generating a response, including tone, goals, and examples, and takes priority over user input. The role hierarchy of developer, user, and assistant mirrors function definitions and arguments in programming, where developer messages establish the system rules and user messages supply the inputs. Few-shot learning steers behavior without retraining by including a handful of input and output examples directly in the prompt; the guide advises using diverse example inputs paired with the desired outputs, typically placed in developer messages and delimited with structured XML and Markdown formatting to keep logical boundaries clear. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses knowledge limits by adding additional relevant context to the generation request, which is essential when the model needs proprietary data or a constrained information set, and it stresses planning for the token-based context window, whose size varies by model, so there is enough capacity for the relevant information. For complex agentic workflows it recommends planning and persistence: instruct the model to resolve the full query before yielding control, decomposing it into sub-tasks and reflecting after each tool call, and to track progress through a TODO list to maintain structured planning. The guide, dated 2025-02-12 in its references, also distinguishes reasoning models, which perform best with high-level guidance, from GPT models, which benefit from very precise instructions that explicitly provide the logic and data.

title: Service Level Objectives, Google SRE Book (Chris Jones, John Wilkes, Niall Richard Murphy, Cody Smith)
text: Chapter 4 of the Google SRE Book distinguishes three related terms that DevOps and SRE engineers frequently conflate. A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service, such as request latency, error rate expressed as a fraction of all requests, system throughput measured in requests per second, and availability, which is often defined as the fraction of well-formed requests that succeed, sometimes called yield. SLIs should measure what users actually experience, and where direct measurement is impossible a proxy may be used. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a target value or range for an SLI, expressed as SLI is less than or equal to target or as a bounded range, with a worked example that 99 percent of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100 ms. The chapter urges choosing objectives with high percentiles such as the 99th or 99.9th rather than averages, because tail latencies matter to user experience, and warns against picking targets based only on current performance or on absolute perfection, favoring realistic and defensible objectives. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is an explicit contract with users that includes consequences, typically financial, for missing the SLOs it contains; the key distinction is that if there are no explicit consequences for missing an objective, you are dealing with an SLO and not an SLA. Error budgets allow SLOs to be violated at a tracked rate so that overly conservative practices do not stifle innovation, creating a control loop in which monitoring SLIs informs decisions about which system improvements are needed.

title: Embracing Risk, Google SRE Book (Marc Alvidrez, ed. Kavita Guliani)
text: The Embracing Risk chapter of the Google SRE Book challenges the assumption that systems should aim for perfect uptime, arguing that extreme reliability comes at a cost because maximizing stability limits how fast new features can be developed. Beyond a certain point each incremental improvement in reliability can cost about 100 times more than the previous increment while delivering value users cannot even perceive: a smartphone user on 99 percent reliable hardware cannot tell the difference between 99.99 percent and 99.999 percent service availability, because other links in the chain dominate the experience. On measurement, Google originally computed time-based availability as uptime over total time, then shifted to a request-based metric, the proportion of successful requests over a rolling window, which works better for globally distributed services that are almost always partially up somewhere. As a worked example, a system serving 2.5 million requests a day with a 99.99 percent availability target can tolerate up to 250 errors while still meeting its objective. The chapter's central tool is the error budget, which quantifies the permissible unreliability over a period such as a quarter: when the product team and the SRE team agree on an SLO, say 99.999 percent quarterly success, the difference between that and 100 percent is the budget of how much unreliability remains for the quarter. This shared metric removes politics from release decisions, since teams can ship freely while budget remains and must redirect effort toward reliability as the budget nears depletion, creating mutual accountability across the organizations. The chapter was written by Marc Alvidrez and edited by Kavita Guliani, with the error budget section contributed by Mark Roth.

title: DORA metrics: the four keys (DORA, a Google Cloud research program, dora.dev)
text: The DORA guide describes software delivery performance metrics that grew from the original four keys into a current model of five metrics spanning two dimensions, throughput and instability. The throughput metrics measure how quickly changes move through the system. Change lead time is the amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed in production. Deployment frequency is the number of deployments over a given period, or equivalently the time between deployments. Failed deployment recovery time is the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention. The instability metrics measure deployment safety. Change fail rate is the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment, typically resulting in rollbacks or hotfixes. Deployment rework rate is the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production. A central research finding is that speed and stability are not tradeoffs: top performers excel across all of these metrics simultaneously rather than trading velocity for reliability, contradicting the conventional assumption that faster delivery must come at the expense of stability. The guide directs readers seeking specific performance benchmark bands to the DORA research section and the Quick Check assessment tool rather than listing thresholds inline. The content is published by DORA, a Google Cloud research program, is licensed CC BY 4.0, and was last updated January 5, 2026.

title: Web Vitals (web.dev, Google)
text: Core Web Vitals are the subset of Web Vitals from Google that apply to all web pages and measure real-world user experience across loading, interactivity, and visual stability. There are three core metrics, each with a recommended threshold. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading performance and should occur within 2.5 seconds of when the page first starts loading. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness to user input and should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability during rendering and should be maintained at 0.1 or less. All three metrics are evaluated the same way, at the 75th percentile of page loads and segmented across mobile and desktop devices, so that a passing score means most users have a good experience. INP replaced the earlier First Input Delay (FID) metric: INP was first introduced as an experimental metric to address runtime performance more comprehensively than FID could, then moved through a pending stage, became stable in 2024, and ultimately retired FID. The guide describes a lifecycle framework in which prospective metrics move through three phases: experimental metrics still undergoing testing, pending metrics that have proven their efficacy and are awaiting ecosystem adaptation, and stable metrics that are finalized and actively supported across Google tools. This page on web.dev was last updated October 31, 2024.

title: Thinking in React (react.dev, official React documentation)
text: The official React documentation lays out a five-step process for building a user interface with React. Step one, break the UI into a component hierarchy, means drawing boxes around every component and subcomponent in a mockup and arranging them into a tree, ideally so each component follows the single-responsibility principle and maps cleanly onto a well-structured data model. Step two, build a static version in React, means constructing components that render the data model using props passed down the hierarchy, without any interactivity or state yet, relying on one-way data flow from parent to child. Step three, find the minimal but complete representation of UI state, applies three questions to each piece of data to decide whether it is state: does it remain unchanged over time, is it passed in from a parent via props, and can it be computed from existing state or props; only data that fails all three tests is genuinely state, following the Don't Repeat Yourself principle by computing derived values on demand rather than storing them. Step four, identify where your state should live, means finding every component that renders based on a piece of state, locating their closest common parent, and placing the state there or in a component above it, since only the owning component can update it. Step five, add inverse data flow, means passing state setter functions down as props so that child components can call them, typically from onChange handlers, to update state that lives higher up. Underlying all of this is the distinction that props are arguments passed from parent to child while state is a component's memory, and React's one-way data flow with a single source of truth makes changes explicit and predictable rather than relying on implicit two-way binding.

title: WAI-ARIA basics (MDN Web Docs)
text: WAI-ARIA, the Web Accessibility Initiative's Accessible Rich Internet Applications specification, is a W3C set of HTML attributes that add semantics to improve accessibility where native HTML features fall short. MDN stresses that ARIA attributes do not change page structure, the DOM, or styling; they only alter the information exposed through the browser's accessibility APIs that assistive technologies such as screen readers consume, and ARIA should be used sparingly, only to fill gaps that native HTML cannot. ARIA provides three feature categories. Roles define what an element is or does, including landmark roles that mirror semantic elements, for example role navigation for nav, role banner for header, and role complementary for aside, as well as widget roles with no direct HTML equivalent such as tablist, tabpanel, and slider. Properties give elements extra meaning that is usually static, such as aria-required on a mandatory input, aria-label to supply an accessible name without visible text, aria-labelledby, and aria-describedby. States describe current conditions that change via JavaScript, such as aria-disabled, aria-live, aria-atomic, and aria-relevant. MDN highlights key principles: prefer native HTML elements like button, nav, and label before reaching for ARIA; never override the native semantics of an element; ensure all interactive controls are keyboard usable, using tabindex 0 to make elements tabbable and tabindex -1 for programmatic focus; announce dynamic updates using aria-live with the value polite to announce when the user is idle or assertive to announce immediately; and test with real assistive-technology users. The aria-live property turns an element into a live region, and pairing it with aria-atomic true reads the whole region as a unit while aria-relevant all announces both additions and removals; role alert automatically creates an assertive live region, which is useful for form validation errors.

title: TestPyramid, by Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com)
text: The Test Pyramid, a term Martin Fowler credits to Mike Cohn's book Succeeding with Agile, is a way to think about how to group automated tests by granularity. Its essential point is that you should have many more low-level unit tests than high-level end-to-end tests running through a GUI. The pyramid has three layers: a broad base of unit tests, a middle layer of service or integration tests, and a narrow apex of UI or end-to-end tests. Fowler recommends subcutaneous tests that operate through the application's service layer as an intermediate strategy, and in a web context this means driving tests through API layers rather than exclusively through browser automation tools like Selenium, reserving GUI-level testing for top-level validation only. He explains why UI tests are problematic: broad-stack tests running through the GUI are brittle, expensive to write, and time consuming to run. UI automation resists change in the system, often requires specialized or licensed tooling, frequently cannot run headless in a deployment pipeline, and even when well built remains more prone to non-determinism problems that undermine confidence. Fowler also warns about the inverted anti-pattern, the ice-cream cone, in which an organization over-invests in high-level UI-driven tests and neglects lower-level coverage, typically by adopting record-playback tooling without building a foundation of unit tests, leaving the team dependent on fragile and slow automation whose maintenance cost balloons whenever the system evolves. The page was originally written on May 1, 2012.

title: Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests, by Mike Wacker (Google Testing Blog)
text: In this Google Testing Blog post, Mike Wacker argues against over-reliance on end-to-end tests and recommends a pyramid-shaped distribution of roughly 70 percent unit tests, 20 percent integration tests, and 10 percent end-to-end tests, while noting that the exact split should reflect each product's particular challenges and risks. He identifies three major problems with leaning too heavily on end-to-end (E2E) tests. First, they are slow to run compared with unit tests, which delays feedback to developers and slows release cycles; unit tests can give sub-second feedback while E2E tests often take hours. Second, they are unreliable and flaky, frequently failing for reasons unrelated to real bugs, such as environmental issues, timing problems, or brittleness in the test framework, which erodes trust in the results. Third, debugging E2E failures is expensive because a single failure could originate anywhere in the entire system, making root-cause analysis difficult and time consuming. Underpinning the recommendation is the fast feedback principle: quick feedback lets developers catch and fix errors before they check in code, and the large difference in feedback speed between unit tests and E2E tests directly affects development velocity and productivity. Wacker concludes that a pyramid strategy that pushes most testing down to fast, reliable unit tests, reserving E2E tests for a small number of critical user workflows that genuinely need full-system validation, is more pragmatic than an E2E-heavy approach for most organizations. The post was published on April 22, 2015.

title: The Practical Test Pyramid, by Ham Vocke (martinfowler.com)
text: Ham Vocke's The Practical Test Pyramid revisits Mike Cohn's model as a visual guide that organizes tests by granularity, with the two enduring takeaways being to write tests with different granularity and that the more high-level you get, the fewer tests you should have. The traditional three layers are unit tests at the base, service or integration tests in the middle, and UI or end-to-end tests at the apex, a shape that guards against the test ice-cream-cone anti-pattern of too many high-level tests. Vocke describes the categories concretely. Unit tests exercise a single unit such as a function or class in isolation, often replacing collaborators with test doubles like stubs and mocks. Integration tests verify interactions at system boundaries such as databases, the filesystem, and external services, testing one integration point at a time, and he distinguishes broad integration tests that are slow and hit real networked dependencies from narrow integration tests that run fast against local test doubles, recommending the narrow approach. UI and end-to-end tests validate complete workflows through the user interface or through a REST API. His central discipline is to push your tests as far down the pyramid as you can, which avoids duplication and keeps the pipeline fast: when a higher-level test fails without a corresponding lower-level failure, you should add a lower-level test to isolate the problem more precisely. He also covers consumer-driven contract tests, using a tool such as Pact, so that services can verify their interfaces remain compatible across team boundaries without requiring full end-to-end integration. The article was published on February 26, 2018.
